title: Glückel of Hameln
hook: a merchant widow writes her memoir in Yiddish for her children

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yiddish: the mother tongue beside the holy tongue. Your line was mama loshen. Today, a mother who wrote in that tongue, at night, for her children.

Hamburg, late at night. The house is quiet, the children asleep. A widow sits up with a pen because she cannot sleep. Her husband, her partner in business and in everything else, has died, and the long nights are the worst part. So she begins to write. Not a book of law or a commentary, but her own life: her childhood, her marriage, the deals and journeys, the births and the deaths, the stories she wants her children to keep.
screen: `A WIDOW AWAKE IN HAMBURG.` → `SHE CANNOT SLEEP.` → `SO SHE WRITES HER LIFE.`

segments.voice: Glückel wrote in Yiddish, and she tells us why: to ease her grief through the sleepless nights, and so that her children would know where they came from. She was not a scholar or a rabbi's daughter writing for the learned. She was a businesswoman. Her husband Chaim dealt in gold and jewels, and she worked beside him; he asked her advice, she says, on everything. After his death she ran the business herself, dealing with creditors, traveling to trade fairs, arranging her children's marriages. All of it goes into the memoir, alongside plague, debts, family quarrels and moments of deep faith. She fills it with moral stories too, and one of them sticks. A father bird has to carry his three chicks across a wide river. Halfway over, he asks the first: when I'm old, will you carry me like this? Yes, says the chick. The father drops it, saying it's a lie. The second chick says yes too, and goes the same way. The third says: I can't promise that. But I will carry my own children like this. That one the father carries safely to the other shore. Glückel tells it with a wry honesty. She doesn't ask her children to repay her. She asks them to pass it on. Why does her book matter here? Many of the voices in recent days have been rabbis and chroniclers. Glückel lets us hear a Jewish home from the inside, in the voice of the woman who ran it.
screen: `WRITTEN AT NIGHT, IN YIDDISH.` · `A BUSINESSWOMAN, NOT A SCHOLAR.` · `THE FATHER BIRD AND THREE CHICKS.` · then, large: `CARRY YOUR OWN CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: If you can, take a scrap of paper or open a note on your phone. Let one small scene from your family come up, a kitchen, a journey, something someone said that you never forgot, and write it in two or three plain sentences, the way Glückel did, for someone who comes after you.
Glückel. A Jewish businesswoman and widow in Hamburg who wrote her life story in Yiddish for her children, to ease her grief. Today's word.
Your line: a woman's memoir. Written at night, for the children who came after. That's day nine hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Glückel's memoir is still read in Yiddish and in translation, and some Jewish families keep the custom of an ethical will, a letter of memories and values left for children.
